facts.statement: Laevisuchus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Laevisuchus (, "light crocodile") is a genus of theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Fossils were discovered by Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur in central India and described by Huene and Matley in 1933.
facts.quote: Its remains were discovered by Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur in Maastrichtian "Carnosaur Bed" deposits in the Lameta Formation in Madhya Pradesh, central India, and were named and described by paleontologists Friedrich von Huene and Matley in 1933.

facts.statement: The genus name combines the Latin word for 'light' and the Greek name for the Egyptian crocodile god Soukhos.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Latin laevis, "light" and the Greek name for the ancient Egyptian crocodile god, Soukhos.

facts.statement: The animal is known from three cervical vertebrae and one dorsal vertebra.
facts.quote: It is known only from three cervical vertebrae (GSI K20/613, GSI K20/614, and GSI K27/696) and a dorsal vertebra (GSI K27/588).

facts.statement: Most fossils were lost until one cervical vertebra was rediscovered in 2012.
facts.quote: All remains except GSI K27/696 were lost, though GSI K20/613 was rediscovered in 2012.

facts.statement: Laevisuchus was a small bipedal carnivore estimated to be about 2 meters long.
facts.quote: Laevisuchus was a small bipedal carnivore about the same size as Masiakasaurus, which is estimated to be around 2 m in length.

facts.statement: One vertebra features a neural arch that is significantly broader and longer than the centrum, giving it a top-heavy appearance.
facts.quote: GSI K27/696 features a neural arch significantly broader and longer than the centrum, creating a top-heavy look.

facts.statement: Recent analysis classifies Laevisuchus as a member of the Noasauridae family.
facts.quote: In 2024, Laevisuchus was recovered as a member of the Noasauridae, in an unresolved position outside the clade that includes Masiakasaurus and Noasaurus.

facts.statement: It lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian in what is now the Indian subcontinent.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico superior, hace aproximadamente 70 millones de años, en el Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es el subcontinente indio.

facts.statement: Estimates suggest it grew to 2 meters long, 90 centimeters high, and weighed about 30 kilograms.
facts.quote: Se calcula que llegó a medir 2 metros de largo, 90 centímetros de alto y a pesar unos 30 kilogramos.

facts.statement: The fossil record spans from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: A 2004 analysis identified it as an abelisauroid based on long epipophyses, foramina on the centrum, and low triangular neural spines.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, un análisis realizado en 2004 ha demostrado que es un abelisauroide debido a sus largas epífitas, un par de agujeros en el centro y las espinas neurales bajas y triangulares.

rejected.statement: A 2024 revision suggested that related taxa like Compsosuchus solus and Ornithomimoides barasimlensis are likely indeterminate abelisaurs.
rejected.quote: A 2024 revision of the small-bodied theropods from India classified Jubbulpuria tenuis as a junior synonym of Laevisuchus, and suggested that other taxa (Compsosuchus solus and Ornithomimoides? barasimlensis) are likely indeterminate abelisaurs.
